title: Classes and Objects
summary: Define your own types with class, __init__, attributes, methods, and readable string forms.
intro: Lists, dicts, and tuples hold data, but the code that works on that data lives somewhere else. A class bundles both into your own type: objects that carry their attributes and the methods that use them.

steps.title: class and __init__
steps.body:
A class defines a new type of value. `__init__` runs every time you create an object, and it stores the starting data on `self`, the new object being built:

```python
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age


rex = Dog("Rex", 3)
```

Calling the class like a function creates an object, also called an instance. Python passes the new object in as `self` for you, so you only pass `name` and `age`. Each `self.name = ...` line makes an instance attribute, and every object gets its own set of them.

Read an attribute with `obj.attr` and change it with `obj.attr = value`:

```python
print(rex.name)  # Rex
rex.age = 4
print(rex.age)  # 4
```

Name classes in PascalCase. Watch the `self.` prefix: writing `name = name` inside `__init__` only makes a local variable that disappears when `__init__` ends, so the object never gets that attribute.

example.title: Two dogs
example.prompt: Define a Dog class, create two dogs, print their attributes, then change one dog's age.
example.code:
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age


rex = Dog("Rex", 3)
bella = Dog("Bella", 5)
print(rex.name, rex.age)
print(f"{bella.name} is {bella.age} years old")
rex.age = 4
print(f"{rex.name} is now {rex.age}")
print(f"{bella.name} is still {bella.age}")
example.output:
Rex 3
Bella is 5 years old
Rex is now 4
Bella is still 5
example.explanation: `Dog("Rex", 3)` runs `__init__` with `self` set to the new object, so `rex` gets its own `name` and `age`. `bella` is a separate object with separate attributes. Setting `rex.age = 4` changes only Rex, which is why Bella still prints 5.

practice.title: Two books
practice.prompt:
Define a Book class and create two books.

1. Give `Book` an `__init__(self, title, author, pages)` that stores all three as attributes.
2. Create `book1 = Book("Dune", "Frank Herbert", 412)` and `book2 = Book("Emma", "Jane Austen", 474)`.
3. Print each book as `<title> by <author>, <pages> pages`.
4. Set `book1.pages` to `896`, then print `<title> now has <pages> pages` for `book1`.

Expected output:

```text
Dune by Frank Herbert, 412 pages
Emma by Jane Austen, 474 pages
Dune now has 896 pages
```
practice.starter:
class Book:
    # TODO: add __init__(self, title, author, pages) that stores all three
    pass


# TODO: create book1 and book2
# TODO: print each book's details
# TODO: set book1.pages to 896 and print the update
practice.solution:
class Book:
    def __init__(self, title, author, pages):
        self.title = title
        self.author = author
        self.pages = pages


book1 = Book("Dune", "Frank Herbert", 412)
book2 = Book("Emma", "Jane Austen", 474)
print(f"{book1.title} by {book1.author}, {book1.pages} pages")
print(f"{book2.title} by {book2.author}, {book2.pages} pages")
book1.pages = 896
print(f"{book1.title} now has {book1.pages} pages")

tests.output:
Dune by Frank Herbert, 412 pages
Emma by Jane Austen, 474 pages
Dune now has 896 pages

hints: Inside `__init__`, write one `self.attr = param` line per parameter.
Read attributes inside an f-string, such as `{book1.title}`, and write one `print()` per line.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
A method is a function defined inside the class. Its first parameter, named `self` by convention, is the object the method was called on. Call it with `obj.method(args)` and Python passes `obj` as `self` for you:

```python
class Tally:
    def __init__(self):
        self.value = 0

    def add(self, n):
        self.value += n

    def doubled(self):
        return self.value * 2


tally = Tally()
tally.add(5)
print(tally.doubled())  # 10
```

Methods do two jobs. Some change the object's attributes, like `add()` updating `self.value`. Others compute and return a result, like `doubled()`. A method can also do both, for example change the object and return `True` or `False` to say whether it worked.

Keeping the data and the code that changes it together means every object updates itself the same way. Inside a method, always reach attributes through `self`. If you forget `self` in the `def` line, the call fails:

```python
# def add(n): ...
# tally.add(5)  # TypeError: Tally.add() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given
```

example.title: Bank account
example.prompt: Write a BankAccount class with deposit, withdraw, and report methods, then run a few transactions.
example.explanation: `deposit()` changes `self.balance` and returns nothing. `withdraw()` refuses an amount larger than the balance and returns `False` without touching it, so only the $30 withdrawal goes through. `report()` changes nothing and returns a string, which the last line prints: 100 + 50 - 30 is 120.

4. Make `total()` return the sum of all the prices.

steps.title: __str__ and __repr__
steps.body:
Print an object from a plain class and you get its type and memory address, which changes every run:

```python
# print(p)  # <__main__.Point object at 0x7f...>
```

Two special methods fix that. Both take only `self` and must return a string.

- `__str__` is the friendly form. `print(obj)`, `str(obj)`, and `f"{obj}"` use it.
- `__repr__` is the unambiguous form for debugging, ideally looking like the code that builds the object. `repr(obj)` and `f"{obj!r}"` use it, and so does a list or dict that holds the object when you print it.

```python
def __str__(self):
    return f"({self.x}, {self.y})"

def __repr__(self):
    return f"Point(x={self.x}, y={self.y})"
```

If a class defines only `__repr__`, `print()` falls back to it, so `__repr__` is the one to write first. Inside `__repr__`, `{self.name!r}` puts quotes around a string attribute, which keeps `Pet('Rex')` readable as code. Python calls these methods for you, so you write `print(p)` or `str(p)`, not `p.__str__()`.

example.title: Printable points
example.prompt: Give Point a friendly __str__ and a debugging __repr__, then print a point several ways.
example.output:
(1, 2)
Start at (1, 2)
Point(x=1, y=2)
[Point(x=1, y=2), Point(x=3, y=4)]
example.explanation: `print(p)` and `str(p)` call `__str__`, giving `(1, 2)`. The `!r` in `f"{p!r}"` switches to `__repr__`. Printing the list calls `__repr__` on each point inside it, which is why the last line shows `Point(x=...)` and not `(1, 2)`.

practice.title: Playing cards
practice.prompt:
Give a Card class readable string forms.

1. Make `__str__` return `<rank> of <suit>`, such as `Q of hearts`.
2. Make `__repr__` return `Card('<rank>', '<suit>')`, with quotes around both strings.
3. Print `card`, then print `You drew the ` + `str(card)`.
4. Print `card` with `!r` in an f-string, then print the list `hand`.

Expected output:

```text
Q of hearts
You drew the Q of hearts
Card('Q', 'hearts')
[Card('Q', 'hearts'), Card('7', 'spades')]
```
practice.solution:
class Card:
    def __init__(self, rank, suit):
        self.rank = rank
        self.suit = suit

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.rank} of {self.suit}"

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Card({self.rank!r}, {self.suit!r})"


card = Card("Q", "hearts")
hand = [card, Card("7", "spades")]
print(card)
print("You drew the " + str(card))
print(f"{card!r}")
print(hand)

tests.output:
Q of hearts
You drew the Q of hearts
Card('Q', 'hearts')
[Card('Q', 'hearts'), Card('7', 'spades')]

hints: `__str__` returns an f-string built from `self.rank` and `self.suit`.
In `__repr__`, `{self.rank!r}` prints the rank with quotes: `'Q'`.
`print(hand)` uses `__repr__` for each card, so you do not need a loop.

steps.title: Class attributes and class methods
steps.body:
A variable assigned in the class body, outside any method, is a class attribute. There is one copy, shared by every instance. Read it with `ClassName.attr`. `self.attr` also finds it when the object has no attribute of that name.

Update a class attribute through the class, as in `Student.count += 1`. Writing `self.count += 1` reads the shared value, then creates a new attribute on that one object, so the class value never moves:

```python
class Team:
    wins = 0

    def win(self):
        self.wins += 1  # bug: should be Team.wins += 1


a = Team()
a.win()
print(a.wins, Team.wins)  # 1 0
```

A mutable class attribute is a trap. With `items = []` in the class body, every object shares one list, and appending through one changes them all. Create lists in `__init__` with `self.items = []`.

`@classmethod` passes the class as `cls` instead of an object. Its main use is an alternative constructor that builds an object from other data and returns `cls(...)`:

```python
@classmethod
def from_string(cls, text):
    name, score = text.split(",")
    return cls(name, int(score))
```

`@staticmethod` gets neither `self` nor `cls`. It is a plain helper that belongs with the class, called as `Student.is_passing(90)`.

example.title: Student counter
example.prompt: Count Student objects with a class attribute, build students from strings, and check scores with a static helper.
example.explanation: `count` lives on the class, and every `__init__` adds 1 to `Student.count`, so creating three students gives 3 no matter how each was built. `from_string` splits the text, converts the score with `int()`, and calls `cls(...)`, which runs `__init__`. `is_passing` needs no object, so it is called on the class.

practice.title: Order counter
practice.prompt:
Count Order objects and add two helper methods.

1. Add a class attribute `count` that starts at `0`, and add 1 to it through the class in `__init__`.

3. Add a `@staticmethod` `is_valid_qty(qty)` that returns `True` when `qty` is from 1 to 10.
4. Create `Order.from_string("pizza,2")`, `Order("soda", 3)`, and `Order.from_string("salad,1")`.
5. Print the first order as `<item> x<qty>`, then `Orders: ` with the count, then `Order.is_valid_qty(2)` and `Order.is_valid_qty(0)` on one line.

Expected output:

```text
pizza x2

```

A static method has no `self` or `cls`. A chained comparison checks both ends of the range at once.

recap:
- `class Name:` defines a type, and calling `Name(...)` creates an object.
- `__init__(self, ...)` sets instance attributes with `self.attr = value`.
- Read and change attributes with `obj.attr` and `obj.attr = value`.
- Methods take `self` first. Call them as `obj.method()`.
- `__str__` serves `print()`, `str()`, and `f"{obj}"`. `__repr__` serves `repr()`, `f"{obj!r}"`, and objects inside printed lists.
- Without either, printing an object shows a memory address.
- Class attributes are shared. Update them with `ClassName.attr`, never `self.attr += ...`.
- Never use a mutable class attribute like `items = []` for per-object data.
- `@classmethod` gets `cls` and builds alternative constructors. `@staticmethod` is a helper with no `self` or `cls`.
